samples.summary: `secureCookies` still returns true for `NODE_ENV=production` regardless of scheme, so a production image served over plain http sets `Secure`/`__Host-` login cookies the browser discards — browser login dead-ends and the CLI consent page loops forever
samples.evidence: `function secureCookies(configService) { if (process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production') return true; const callbackUrl = ...startsWith('https://'); }`. The OR with NODE_ENV contradicts the stated rule (`docs/design/backend.md:384`: "it is not keyed to `NODE_ENV`: it applies whenever `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL` is `https://`"). `Dockerfile:88` sets `ENV NODE_ENV=production`, and `packages/documentation/developers/self-hosting.md:42` / `README.md:126` document `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL=http://localhost:3000/auth/github/callback`. On that combination `loginCookieName` yields `__Host-…` and `loginCookieOptions.secure=true`; browsers reject `Secure`/`__Host-` cookies from an http origin, so (a) `verifyCallbackState`'s web branch never finds `OAUTH_STATE_COOKIE` and every callback redirects to `/login?error=login_state`, and (b) `GitHubAuthGuard.hasConfirmation` never sees `wafflebase_cli_confirm`, so clicking Continue on the consent page just re-renders a fresh consent page — an unbreakable loop with no error text. Making the check scheme-first (or `secureCookies = https-callback || (production && !http-callback)`) avoids it.

samples.summary: Two concurrent CLI logins (or two concurrent browser logins) in one browser collide on the single-named state/confirm cookies: the second start overwrites the first's binding and the first callback is refused as a forgery
samples.evidence: `browserBinding: this.issueLoginCookie(context, CLI_STATE_COOKIE)` writes the fixed name `wafflebase_cli_state`; `issueLoginCookie(context, CLI_CONFIRM_COOKIE)` likewise, and the browser flow writes the fixed `OAUTH_STATE_COOKIE` at line 360. The comment at github-auth.guard.ts:22-29 argues separate names are needed precisely because "one shared name means the second start overwrites the first's binding and the first callback is refused as a forgery, which is a login that fails for a reason no one can see" — but that reasoning applies unchanged to two `wafflebase login` runs, or to a user opening the login page in two tabs. `verifyCallbackState` (auth.controller.ts:314-328) then throws BadRequestException for the first CLI callback and its CLI waits out the full 5-minute `CALLBACK_TIMEOUT_MS`; the browser case redirects to `/login?error=login_state`. Nothing keys the cookie name (or a map inside one cookie) to the individual login.

samples.summary: The single-use `/launch/<token>` redirect has no recovery path: any consumer other than the user's browser (link scanner, prefetch, opener probe, a second window) burns the token and the real browser gets a bare 404
samples.evidence: `launchTarget = undefined;` after the first successful GET means a second request to the same URL falls into the `!launchTarget` branch and returns `res.writeHead(404); res.end('Not found')`. The user has no way to retry — the authorization URL is only in the (owner-only) `login-url.txt` on non-TTY stderr, and on a TTY it was printed before the hop, so a TTY user who loses the race sees only a 404 page and then a five-minute wait. Given the URL is handed to an arbitrary system opener (`openBrowser`), a duplicate dereference is not far-fetched.

samples.summary: `openBrowser` attaches the `error` listener after `await open(url)`, which may be too late to absorb the spawn ENOENT it exists for
samples.evidence: `const child = await open(url); child?.on?.('error', () => {});`. `child_process.spawn` schedules a spawn failure with `process.nextTick(onErrorNT, ...)` synchronously at spawn time, and Node drains the nextTick queue before promise microtasks, so the `error` event can be emitted before the awaited promise's continuation runs and attaches the listener — in which case the EventEmitter rethrows and the CLI dies mid-login, exactly the failure the helper documents. The new test (`login-callback.test.ts`, `absorbs the child process error…`) emits manually after the await and therefore cannot observe this ordering.

samples.summary: Raising the callback timeout to 5 minutes means every failed CLI login now blocks the terminal for five minutes instead of thirty seconds, because the backend's refusals never reach the listener
samples.evidence: `export const CALLBACK_TIMEOUT_MS = 5 * 60 * 1000;`. When `verifyCallbackState` throws BadRequestException for a CLI callback (auth.controller.ts:326) or the guard 400s the start, nothing is ever sent to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback`, so `waitForCallback` can only settle via the timeout. The same applies to the `sawUnboundCode` diagnostic, which is only surfaced at line 458-467 — i.e. after five minutes of silence. A pending-failure signal (or a shorter idle timeout before any browser hit) would keep the diagnosis timely.

samples.summary: Post-listen server errors call `reject` on an already-settled promise and are swallowed, leaving the login hanging until the (now 5-minute) timeout
samples.evidence: `srv.on('error', (err) => { if (err.code === 'EADDRINUSE' && attempts < 3) tryListen(); else reject(err); })` — after `resolve(...)` has run inside the `listen` callback, any later server error (or a 4th EADDRINUSE) hits a no-op `reject`, so `callbackPromise` never rejects and the command waits out `CALLBACK_TIMEOUT_MS`. Routing post-listen errors to `callbackReject` would surface them.

samples.summary: `failFromBackend` writes the envelope with `console.error` and immediately calls `process.exit`, which can truncate the line when stderr is a pipe — the exact agent-harness case the envelope is for
samples.evidence: `console.error(backendErrorEnvelope(...)); return process.exit(code === 'HTTP_ERROR' ? 1 : 2);`. On POSIX, writes to a pipe are asynchronous, so `process.exit()` may terminate before the queued write flushes and the caller sees a non-zero exit with no envelope at all. Setting `process.exitCode` and returning (as the other CLI error paths do via `outputError`) avoids the race.

samples.summary: `runCli` registers a `preAction` hook on every invocation, so a reused program accumulates hooks and `acting` can be stale from a prior parse
samples.evidence: `program.hook('preAction', (_thisCommand, actionCommand) => { acting = actionCommand; });` runs inside `runCli`, whose `program` parameter defaults to a fresh `buildProgram()` but is explicitly overridable (and is overridden in tests). Calling `runCli(sharedProgram, …)` twice registers the hook twice; more importantly, if a later parse throws before any action runs (a usage error), `acting` still holds whatever subcommand ran previously, so `outputError` attributes the failure to the wrong command. Registering the hook once at `buildProgram` time, or resetting `acting` before `parseAsync`, would fix it.

samples.summary: `loginErrorUrl` produces a same-origin backend path when `FRONTEND_URL` is unset, redirecting the failed login to a backend 404 instead of the login page
samples.evidence: `const base = (this.configService.get<string>('FRONTEND_URL') ?? '').replace(/\/$/, ''); return `${base}/login?error=…`;`. With `FRONTEND_URL` missing this yields `/login?error=login_state`, which the browser resolves against the backend origin — a 404 with no path back. The success path (line 268) uses `configService.get('FRONTEND_URL')!` and would at least fail loudly; the error path silently degrades.

The OR with NODE_ENV contradicts the stated rule (`docs/design/backend.md:384`: "it is not keyed to `NODE_ENV`: it applies whenever `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL` is `https://`"). `Dockerfile:88` sets `ENV NODE_ENV=production`, and `packages/documentation/developers/self-hosting.md:42` / `README.md:126` document `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL=http://localhost:3000/auth/github/callback`. On that combination `loginCookieName` yields `__Host-…` and `loginCookieOptions.secure=true`; browsers reject `Secure`/`__Host-` cookies from an http origin, so (a) `verifyCallbackState`'s web branch never finds `OAUTH_STATE_COOKIE` and every callback redirects to `/login?error=login_state`, and (b) `GitHubAuthGuard.hasConfirmation` never sees `wafflebase_cli_confirm`, so clicking Continue on the consent page just re-renders a fresh consent page — an unbreakable loop with no error text. verdict.reason: The code is present verbatim as claimed: github-auth.guard.ts:72 short-circuits `secureCookies` to true on NODE_ENV=production before ever consulting the callback scheme, making the effective rule `production || https-callback`. This directly contradicts the invariant stated in its own comment (github-auth.guard.ts:64-69, :246) and in docs/design/backend.md:384-390. The failing combination is a documented, unguarded deployment: Dockerfile:88 sets ENV NODE_ENV=production, while self-hosting.md:42, README.md:126 and packages/backend/README.md:31 all document an http:// GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL, and there is no config validation (no validationSchema/Joi in app.module.ts) tying production to https. On that combination loginCookieName (:142) emits `__Host-` names and loginCookieOptions (:153) sets secure:true, which a browser discards from a plain-http origin; verifyCallbackState's web branch (auth.controller.ts:293-308) then never finds the cookie and every callback redirects to /login?error=login_state (auth.controller.ts:230-232). Separately and independently, cliLoginAvailable (:119-121) is `secureCookies || loopbackCallback`, so on a non-loopback plain-http production origin the documented "refuse CLI login unless https or loopback" guard (:100-118, docs/design/backend.md:386-390) is bypassed, the flow starts, hasConfirmation (:371-383) never matches the discarded prefixed cookie, and canActivate re-renders the consent page (:337-346) — a silent loop with no error. No refutation ground applies: the code is present, no caller or startup check makes it unreachable, and a broken invariant plus a no-error login dead-end is squarely within the correctness lens. The fact that session cookies at auth.controller.ts:490 use the same NODE_ENV convention shows the http-production mode is broken in more than one place, not that this path is guarded.

verdict.reason: Every element of the finding checks out in the repository. Cookie names are fixed constants (github-auth.guard.ts:17,31,37) and loginCookieName (github-auth.guard.ts:138-143) only optionally prefixes `__Host-`; issueLoginCookie (github-auth.guard.ts:393-407) writes that single slot for the CLI confirm (:342), the CLI state binding (:352) and the browser flow (:360), so a second concurrent start of the SAME flow in one browser overwrites the first's value. On the first callback, takeStateCookie (auth.controller.ts:344-349) reads that one name and verifyCallbackState fails the binding compare, throwing BadRequestException for CLI (auth.controller.ts:311-329) — which is rethrown rather than redirected (auth.controller.ts:230-233), leaving the CLI to wait out CALLBACK_TIMEOUT_MS = 5 min (packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:323,470) — or UnauthorizedException for the browser (auth.controller.ts:293-308) turned into /login?error=login_state (auth.controller.ts:231). Nothing keys the cookie name or contents to an individual login, and GET /auth/github is unauthenticated and re-entrant, so no guard or caller makes the collision unreachable. The guard's own comment (github-auth.guard.ts:19-30) makes precisely this argument for two flows while leaving two same-flow starts exposed. Real, reachable, user-visible login failure — correctness lane, at least major.

verdict.reason: The single-use burn (login.ts:376) and the 404 on re-use (login.ts:363-370) exist as quoted, but the finding's stated impact — "no recovery path; the user has no way to retry" — is contradicted by the caller. login.ts:70-71 unconditionally calls `announceLoginUrl(oauthUrl)` with the RAW authorization URL immediately after `armLaunch`, on every login (not just on opener failure). On a TTY, announceLoginUrl prints the full authorization URL to the terminal (login.ts:212-218: "If no browser opened, visit this URL to continue"), which is byte-identical to the 302 Location the launch hop would have produced (login.ts:377-381) and remains valid for the whole CALLBACK_TIMEOUT_MS = 5 min window (login.ts:323). On non-TTY it is written to the 0600 login-url.txt whose path is printed (login.ts:221-233) and which is only deleted in the finally after the callback settles or times out (login.ts:77-82), so it too is available for the entire window. The reviewer's ordering premise is also inverted: the URL is printed after the hop is armed, not before, and in either case it stays in scrollback. Spending the launch token therefore costs the user one paste, not the login; the behavior is the documented, tested tradeoff (login.ts:62-69, 373-375; login-callback.test.ts:83-107), not an unrecoverable dead end. Residual impact is a confusing 404 page with recovery instructions already on screen — not a blocking correctness defect.
